newsitem.title: JAPAN: Prosecutors poised to raid Nomura HQ-media reports.
newsitem.headline: Prosecutors poised to raid Nomura HQ-media reports.

text.p: Prosecutors plan to search the headquarters of Japan's biggest brokerage, Nomura Securities Co Ltd, as early as Tuesday to investigate the firm's suspected illegal payments to a corporate client, Japanese media reported.

The prosecutors' office declined to comment on the unsourced reports, which were carried by Japan's Kyodo and Jiji news agencies. A Nomura spokesman said he was not aware of any raids on the company's offices.

The Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC), Japan's securities watchdog, has been probing Nomura over its March 6 admission that two of its directors made discretionary deals banned under Japanese law and funnelled profits to a corporate client.
The client has been linked by the Japanese media to corporate racketeers, known in Japan as "sokaiya", who extort money from companies by threatening to disrupt annual shareholder meetings.

If Nomura's deals are found to violate a commercial code banning payoffs to racketeers, legal action could be taken against the firm, at the request of the SESC. The scandal has already led to the resignation of Nomura's president and an internal investigation by the company.
The reports of a possible imminent search hit Nomura's share price, which ended the day down 20 yen at 1,440.
But brokers said the impact of the news was limited as the market had been expecting such a development in the Nomura scandal.
"What the market is more concerned about is any punitive measures which will be taken against the brokerage," said Yasuo Ueki, Nikko Securities Co Ltd general manager.
"The punishment will probably have an effect on the firm's business and could have an impact on the whole brokerage industry as well," Ueki said.
The investigation comes six years after leading Japanese brokerages, including Nomura, were hit by a scandal over improper compensation to favoured clients.
Top executives at Nomura and Nikko Securities Co Ltd resigned in 1991 over the improper compensation and revelations that affiliates had done deals with gangsters.

Nomura is already suffering repercussions from the latest scandal, with a number of major clients having suspended business dealings with the brokerage, one of the world's most powerful financial institutions.
